Variegated snailfish Liparis gibbus is a common benthic sculpin of the Arctic marine shelf, where water temperatures routinely hover slightly below the freezing point. Newly hatched individuals emerge from demersal eggs after an extended incubation period of approximately 200 days [ab = approximately 200 days] under the prevailing thermal regime of -0.3 °C [T = -0.3 °C]. The prolarvae at eclosion are remarkably small, weighing only about 0.092 grams [Wwb = about 0.092 grams] as they begin the lecithotrophic yolk absorption stage. This modest initial mass is consistent with the allocation of maternal resources into numerous small offspring, a strategy shared with many cold-water cottids. Following the swim bladder inflation and the onset of exogenous feeding, the exotrophic larvae commence a phase of rapid growth that continues through the larval-juvenile transition. First feeding occurs once the yolk-sac has been largely resorbed, marking the trophic switch to planktonic prey capture. The prolonged incubation period at sub-zero temperatures is a notable feature of the early life history.

As juveniles progress toward the sub-adult phase, the attainment of sexual maturity is marked by a distinct increase in length. Field surveys of spawning populations indicate that puberty is reached at a total length of 4.3 centimeters [Lp = 4.3 centimeters]. Corresponding to this length, an individual at the onset of reproductive capability exhibits a wet weight of 0.98 grams [Wwp = 0.98 grams], derived from a length-weight regression model applied to Arctic specimens. These values place the species among the smaller-bodied members of the genus at the point of first gonadal activation. The shift from immature post-metamorphic juvenile to gravid adult involves substantial somatic growth; individuals must more than double their body mass between the onset of gametogenesis and their first successful contribution to the spawning stock. Vitellogenesis onset and subsequent egg production are tightly coupled to the seasonal availability of benthic amphipod prey. The modest body size at maturation may reflect a life-history trade-off favoring early reproductive output in an environment with high adult mortality risk.

Throughout the adult stage, growth continues but at a decelerated rate, eventually approaching an asymptotic maximum. The ultimate total length attained by Liparis gibbus in the wild has been recorded at 52 centimeters [Li = 52 centimeters], based on the largest individuals sampled in bottom-trawl surveys across the Barents and Chukchi Seas. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fish of this length is estimated at 1967 grams [Wwi = 1967 grams], a value calculated from the species-specific length-mass equation. This asymptotic size is considerable for a snailfish, placing it among the longer-bodied members of its family. The attainment of such a length requires several years of feeding on a diet dominated by hyperiid amphipods and small decapods. Most reproductively active adults in trawl catches measure between 25 and 40 centimeters, suggesting that the largest individuals represent a relatively small fraction of the population. The growth trajectory reflects the constraints of a cold, low-productivity ecosystem where metabolic rates are inherently depressed.

Reproductive output in this iteroparous species is strongly influenced by the thermal environment. Under a stable water temperature of -0.3 °C [T = -0.3 °C], a single female achieves a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 1.37 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1.37 eggs per day]. This daily rate translates into a substantial annual fecundity, with spawning females depositing adhesive demersal egg masses on hard substrates. The eggs are notably large, with a mean diameter of 5.6 millimeters, a trait that contributes to the relatively high birth mass of the prolarvae. Broad-scale surveys indicate that the spawning period extends from late autumn through early winter. The maximum reproductive rate is attained by the largest females, whose larger body cavity accommodates a greater volume of developing oocytes. This relationship between size and fecundity is typical among cold-water marine teleosts, where fecundity scales positively with female length. The combination of large egg size and extended incubation at sub-zero temperatures represents a significant energetic investment per offspring.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] in the natural environment, based on otolith age estimates from specimens collected in the Canadian Arctic at a water temperature of -0.3 °C [T = -0.3 °C]. This value is notable because the asymptotic length implied by the von Bertalanffy growth function for an 8-year-old fish is substantially smaller than the recorded ultimate length of 52 centimeters [Li = 52 centimeters]; most individuals likely die well before they could reach that extreme size. Senescence-related mortality appears to increase sharply after the sixth year of life, with very few individuals surviving beyond eight winters. The species' life history is thus characterized by a relatively fast pace of early growth followed by an extended plateau of reproductive activity. Age-related declines in feeding efficiency or metabolic capacity may contribute to the reduced growth in older individuals. The oldest documented specimen, aged from a sagittal otolith, was a 7.9-year-old female. This maximum longevity is consistent with other high-latitude sculpins that experience low metabolic costs but face predation pressure from seals and larger gadids.
